title: Activation paging and KV staging playbook for NUMA/PCI fabric
body:
Summary
This playbook outlines a runtime strategy to reduce multi GPU inference tail latency caused by NUMA and PCIe fabric boundaries. It combines activation paging, staged KV cache residency, and a lightweight topology biased scheduler. The approach is conservative about reshuffling global ownership and focuses on transient locality improvements, prefetch smoothing, and small, low risk migrations.

Problem statement
Observed issues on production racks: when an activation or KV lookup crosses a CPU socket or traverses a host PCIe root complex, additional latency spikes of 100 to 400 microseconds appear. These spikes disproportionately affect p95 and p99 for medium length requests and single request microbatches. Standard sharding and NCCL default routing assumes homogenous intra node links and does not adapt to short lived locality patterns.

Goals
- Reduce cross-socket and host bounce transfers for latency sensitive requests.
- Provide a mechanism for hot keys to be served locally without changing authoritative ownership semantics.
- Smooth prefetch and promotion traffic to avoid PCIe saturation during bursts.
- Allow NCCL collectives to be biased for latency sensitive microbatches while preserving high throughput for large batched work.

Core concepts
1) Topology map and labels
At agent startup the node daemon builds a topology map that includes: node id, cpu socket id, pci root id, nvlink groups, rdma capability, and a rough peer bandwidth estimate. Each GPU is labelled with a small set of tokens derived from that map which are used by placement heuristics. The map is refreshed periodically and when hardware changes are detected.

2) Residency tiers and metadata
Define four residency tiers: tier0 GPU local, tier1 same root or nvlink group, tier2 other socket same host, tier3 remote host. For each KV entry we store a flat metadata record: residency_tier, last_seen_ts, decay_score. The record is intentionally tiny so caches can be scanned quickly.

3) Activation paging primitives
Two primary primitives are exposed to the kernel execution path: async_prefetch(key, target_gpu) and soft_pin(key, duration_ms). Async prefetch places a DMA task on a prioritized queue. Soft pin attaches a short lived hint that increases the likelihood the scheduler keeps the request on the same GPU or peer set for the next few layers. Pins expire quickly to avoid long term imbalance.

4) Staged promotion and demotion policy
Promote entries only when sustained hotness is observed. Hotness is computed with an exponential decay counter sampled on every access. Promotion work is backgrounded and rate limited by available DMA credits to avoid saturating host links. Demotions are batched and written back lazily to avoid large synchronous host writes. Ephemeral request specific keys are marked transient and not considered for promotion.

5) Micro migration and recompute fallback
When an activation is missing locally and prefetch would exceed latency budget, attempt a local recompute of a short prefix of the layer if the operator supports it. This is a cheap fallback for common small layers. If recompute is not possible, perform a single synchronous transfer but mark the entry for immediate background promotion if its hot_score warrants it. Micro migrations move small numbers of hot entries to a target GPU when both bandwidth and vacancy allow.

6) Topology biased scheduler
For microbatches below a configurable threshold, the scheduler computes a peer score for candidate GPUs: peer_score = w1 * locality_match + w2 * link_bandwidth - w3 * current_load. The scheduler prefers peers that minimize extra hops. If no low hop peers are free, best effort selection is used. For large batches the scheduler falls back to throughput first grouping. Tunables w1,w2,w3 are exposed to ops for quick tuning.

7) DMA crediting and QoS
Each GPU has a small token bucket for prefetch dma work. Tokens are consumed by async_prefetch and slowly refill. If the overall p99 climbs, the refill rate is reduced and aggressive prefetch is curtailed. This prevents storms that cause long tail spikes.

8) Observability and signals
Emit metrics per request: locality score, number of cross socket transfers, prefetch wait time, promotion latency. Track counters for promotions, demotions, rejected prefetches, recompute fallbacks. Use these signals to tune DMA credits and scheduler tunables.

Example request execution flow
1. Planner enumerates layers and required keys for the request.
2. For each key in the upcoming window, consult residency; if tier > 1, submit async_prefetch to tier0 or tier1 targets.
3. Soft_pin frequently accessed keys for the next N ms.
4. Scheduler picks peer set biased by topology labels and current load.
5. Execute kernels; if a missing activation blocks, attempt local recompute, otherwise perform a sync transfer if within budget.
6. At completion update decay_score for touched keys and enqueue promotions if thresholds hit.

Pseudocode snippet
score(peer, request) = alpha * locality(peer, request) + beta * link_bw(peer) - gamma * load(peer)\preferred = topK(gpus, score)\if microbatch_size < MICROTHRESHOLD:
  select preferred\else
  use throughput grouping
end

Safety and correctness
Residency changes are cache hints only. The authoritative store remains unchanged and writes still serialize through the owner. Promotions and demotions must not change correctness semantics. In-flight write operations must invalidate local hints and may trigger synchronous writebacks.

Open questions and follow ups
- Exact thresholds for promotion and demotion tuning per rack type.
- Policies for combining recompute heuristics with operator fusion.
- How to expose tunables to ops safely and fall back to conservative defaults.
- Integration points with NCCL for per-request soft routing without destabilizing global collectives.

Next steps
- Prototype the topology map and residency metadata footprint.
- Implement async_prefetch with DMA crediting and a simple scheduler bias.
- Run microbenchmarks across a mixed NVLink/PCIe lab rack to quantify p95 improvements and promotion overhead.

Notes
This doc is a living playbook intended for the serving runtime team. It is a conservative set of changes aimed at improving latency for latency sensitive short flows while preserving existing throughput behavior for large batched workloads.
